source.title: CUSE: Fine-Grained Multimodal Unlearning with Counterfactual Guidance and On-Policy Self-Distillation
source.authors: Chen-Lu Ding; Jian-Can Wu; Yan-Chen Luo; Tian-Yu Zhang; Yan-Cheng Yuan; Xiang Wang; Xiang-Nan He

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; it is not garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates whether prompt and sampling perturbations restore target information after its own multimodal unlearning method, using behavioural measures different from the cited original sources.
record.gate_note: The paper's Table 3 reports results for CUSE under random-prefix, paraphrase, jailbreak, and sampling-based perturbations; these directly test prompting-related recovery. The paper also reports CUSE's unlearning and retention scores across models and forgetting ratios. Results cited from other work and values used only to choose hyperparameters are not included.
record.test_reason: A new multimodal unlearning method (CUSE) evaluated on MLLMU-Bench (fictitious profiles) with LLaVA-1.5-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Table 1/Table 4 give forget- and retain-set scores against the pre-unlearning model (A). Table 3 gives forget- and retain-set scores under random-prefix, paraphrase, jailbreak and sampling attacks (LLaVA, 5% forget). These are the study's own results on whether unlearning holds under simple attacks (A), whether prompt-only attacks recover forgotten knowledge (E), and whether a newer method resists those attacks (F), in a new setting (MLLMs).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that CUSE forgets effectively and naturally while preserving retained knowledge and multimodal capability. They report that it beats the baselines on MLLMU-Bench and CoVUBench across backbones, and that forgetting holds under random-prefix, paraphrase, jailbreak and sampling perturbations.
record.recipe_differences: CUSE uses counterfactual sensitivity-aware token weighting and dual-branch on-policy self-distillation for multimodal unlearning; it does not test the original sources' recovery attacks such as fine-tuning, activation ablation, or quantization.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that increasing the sensitivity-reweighting coefficient strengthens forgetting but can reduce retained utility; results vary across forgetting ratios. The prompt-perturbation results are reported for LLaVA-1.5-7B.
record.problems: The paper provides no chance-level reference for its classification, ROUGE-L, or cloze measures. The prompt robustness table reports one model and one forgetting ratio, and no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: Other benchmark results, baseline-method comparisons, utility metrics outside the cited rows, and CoVUBench results are omitted because the row budget was reached; see Tables 1, 2, 4, and 5 and Sections 4.2-4.4. Figure-only results and cited findings are also omitted.

untested.parts: Only CUSE is evaluated under attack, and only with prompt and sampling attacks. Relearning, quantization and internal-edit attacks are not tested. No chance level or knowledge probe is given.
No activation ablation, and no analysis of whether the knowledge is deleted or only blocked.
No other-language queries, no in-context information and no image-side perturbations. There is one generic jailbreak prompt style, only LLaVA-1.5-7B at the 5% ratio, and no uncertainty.
Resistance to fine-tuning, quantization and activation ablation, the main attacks in this literature, is not tested. Prompt attacks are tested only on LLaVA-1.5-7B at 5%.

missing.what: Test-set forget scores, i.e. whether forgetting generalizes to held-out variants: LLaVA classification 44.80→14.40, ROUGE-L 0.289→0.009, cloze 26.00→6.00; Qwen classification 65.60→15.00.
Qwen2.5-VL forget ROUGE-L 0.600→0.142 and cloze 36→8, with retain ROUGE-L 0.581→0.579 and retain classification 68.30→66.17.

record.verdict_notes:
Changes from the previous verdict:
(1) Merged the 12 duplicate row_fixes pairs (R11–R33, odd) into one item per row. For the prompt-attack forget rows (R11–R27, odd) the versions are A, E, F with state absent. The state refers to E, the recovery effect against the unperturbed CUSE baseline, and each problem field says that for A and F the same numbers mean forgetting holds.
(2) The text (Appendix B.5) shows that the sampling attack varies decoding configurations, not the prompt. So it is not E's prompting and not one of the attacks F names. R29–R34 are now linked to A only (observed); R29/R31/R33 were removed from the E label and R29–R34 from the F label, and the conditions were updated.
(3) Dropped two missing items, the baseline methods and the CoVUBench results, because the record's rows_left_out declares both. Under the rules, missing covers only undeclared results.
(4) Added R05–R10 (A-linked duplicates) to the unattacked A label and rewrote its reason with exact row ids. Added Qwen retain classification to a missing item.
Everything else is kept: relation, tranche, untested, authors_conclusion, and the remaining states and links.
Substantive caveats, also kept: the reader's V1–V6 map to A–F, and V2 (B) was wrongly attached to the forget rows, since no relearning is tested. R05–R10 and R35–R40 duplicate the Table 1 values. The prompt attacks are weak: fixed neutral prefixes, one generic jailbreak style, GPT paraphrases, one model at one ratio, and no uncertainty reported. The forgetting privileged context trains toward non-disclosure, and the case study's output reads 'I cannot provide information regarding this individual's profession'. So the low forget scores may reflect learned refusal rather than deletion, but the paper does not test this, so C stays untested. MLLMU-Bench classification is multiple choice, and forget accuracy of about 11% may be below chance; the paper states no chance level.

versions.untested_parts: Tests CUSE, not all current unlearning methods. The paper does not state a chance-level reference, so whether its scores are near chance cannot be determined.
No fine-tuning attack or relearning set is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of recovery through an internal edit is reported.
No low-bit quantization attack is tested.
Tests random prefixes, paraphrases, jailbreak prompts, and sampling variations. It does not test other languages or in-context relearning information.
Tests CUSE against the listed prompt and sampling perturbations, but not fine-tuning, internal edits, or quantization attacks.
